title: Self-Dual Test-Vector Normalization For Nested Lattice Models
body_html:
Self-Dual Test-Vector Normalization For Nested Lattice Models

Fix once and for all the Haar measure on $W$ used in all lattice-model integral operators. The normalization convention is:

  • A lattice $L\subset W$ is called self-dual when $L=L^\perp$. Here $L^\perp=\{w\in W:\psi(\langle w,l\rangle_W)=1\;\forall l\in L\}$ is the symplectic dual (orthogonal complement). In the hermitian-setting KB nodes the notation $L^\#$ denotes the metric dual $\{v:h(v,L)\subseteq\mathfrak{o}_D\}$, which is a different object.
  • In the notation of the transition-map problem, the self-dual case is the case $\mathcal{B}_0=\mathcal{B}_{0^+}$.
  • Every self-dual lattice has Haar volume $1$:

$$ \mu(L)=1 \qquad\text{if }L=L^\perp. $$

Thus the Haar measure is not an additional missing choice. If a transition construction still has a scalar ambiguity, the ambiguity must come from the choice of comparison intertwiners, splittings, polarizations, or finite Fourier-transform normalizations, not from an unspecified Haar measure.

Suppose two lattice models are attached to lattices

$$ B_0\subseteq B'_0. $$

Choose a self-dual lattice

$$ A_0\subseteq B_0\subseteq B'_0. $$

The existence of such an $A_0$ is treated as available for good lattices: every good lattice contains a self-dual lattice, and in the nested case one chooses $A_0$ inside the smaller lattice.

Let

$$ \Omega_{A_0}:=\mathcal{S}(A_0) $$

be the lattice model with respect to the self-dual lattice $A_0$. Since $A_0$ is self-dual, its distinguished test vector is the characteristic function

$$ v_{A_0}:=\mathbf{1}_{A_0}\in \Omega_{A_0}. $$

This is the reference test vector. The test line attached to $A_0$ in the $B_0$-lattice model, and likewise in the $B'_0$-lattice model, is defined by comparing those models with $\Omega_{A_0}$ and taking the inverse image of the line $\mathbb{C}\,\mathbf{1}_{A_0}$.

Equivalently, the transition map between the $B_0$- and $B'_0$-models should be normalized by requiring that, after comparison with the $A_0$-model, it carries the vector corresponding to $\mathbf{1}_{A_0}$ to the vector corresponding to $\mathbf{1}_{A_0}$ with scalar $1$.

In the pulled-back facet setting, when an incidence $E\leq F$ gives

$$ L_F\subseteq L_E, $$

the test-vector normalization is applied with

$$ B_0=L_F, \qquad B'_0=L_E. $$

The same test vector can be used to compute the already-defined character $\delta^{\mathrm{lm}}_{E,F}$. For $k\in K_F\subseteq K_E$, compare the actions of the original splittings $s_F(k)$ and $s_E(k)$ on $\mathbf{1}_{A_0}$ after transporting both actions to the $A_0$-model.

More generally, if $kA_0\ne A_0$, compare the two induced maps from $\mathbb{C}\,\mathbf{1}_{A_0}$ in the $A_0$-model to $\mathbb{C}\,\mathbf{1}_{kA_0}$ in the $kA_0$-model. The ratio of these two scalars should recover

$$ \delta^{\mathrm{lm}}_{E,F}(k). $$

The existence of a common reference model or common normalized comparison intertwiners does not by itself imply $\delta^{\mathrm{lm}}_{E,F}=1$. The character compares the already chosen lattice-model splittings $s_F$ and $s_E$.
